title: Closest Leaf in a Binary Tree
statement: You get the `root` of a binary tree in which every node holds a different value, and an integer `k` that is the value of one of its nodes. A leaf is a node with no children. Return the value of the leaf that is nearest to the node holding `k`, where the distance between two nodes is the number of edges on the path joining them (the path may climb up through parents and then go down again). The node holding `k` may itself be a leaf, at distance 0. When several leaves are equally near, returning any one of them is accepted.
constraints: The tree has between 1 and 1000 nodes.
Some node in the tree has Node.val == k.
notes:
## Intuition

Distances in a tree can go up as well as down, so the nearest leaf to the node `k` might sit in a completely different branch. If every node also knew its parent, the tree would be an ordinary undirected graph, and the nearest leaf would simply be the first leaf a breadth-first search from `k` reaches, because BFS visits nodes in order of distance. (A slower idea compares root-to-node paths: the distance between two nodes is the sum of their depths minus twice the depth of their deepest shared ancestor.)

## Approach

1. Walk the whole tree once with a `stack`, recording `parent` for every child and remembering the `target` node whose value is `k`.
2. Start a BFS from `target` with a `queue` and a `seen` set.
3. Take nodes from the front in order. The first node with no children is a nearest leaf; return its value.
4. Otherwise push its unvisited neighbours: `left`, `right` and `parent`.

## Example 1, step by step

`root = [1,3,2]`, `k = 1`. The first walk records that `3` and `2` have parent `1`, and `target` is the root. The BFS starts with `queue = [1]`; node `1` has children, so `3` and `2` are queued. Node `3` comes out next and is a leaf, so the reference returns `3`. Leaf `2` is also one edge away, so the stated answer `2` is equally correct; either value is accepted.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): the walk and the BFS each touch every node at most once.
- Space: O(n) for `parent`, `seen`, the stack and the queue.

## Pitfalls

- Searching only below `k` is wrong: in Example 3 the nearest leaf `3` is reached by going up to the root first.
- Mark nodes as seen when they are queued, otherwise a node and its parent keep queueing each other.
- The node `k` itself can be a leaf; check the node taken from the queue before expanding it, so that case returns at distance 0.
- A leaf has neither child; a node with just one child is not a leaf.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `parent` | map from each node to its parent |
| `stack` | nodes still to visit in the first walk |
| `target` | the node whose value is `k` |
| `queue`, `head` | BFS queue and the index of its front |
| `seen` | nodes already queued |
| `next` | a neighbour: left child, right child or parent |

narration.2: Tree nodes only point down, so record each node's parent to be able to move up too.
narration.3: Walk the whole tree with an explicit stack, starting at the root.
narration.5: Keep going until every node has been visited.
narration.7: Is this the node holding k?
narration.8: Remember it as the BFS starting point.
narration.10: Look at both children of the current node.
narration.12: Record the parent link for this child...
narration.18: Start the breadth-first search at the node holding k.
narration.19: Mark the start as seen so it is never queued again.
narration.20: Take nodes in queue order, which is the order of their distance from k.
narration.22: A node without children is a leaf, and BFS reaches the nearest leaf first.
narration.25: Neighbours in the tree are the two children and the parent.
narration.26: Skip missing neighbours and nodes already queued.
narration.27: Mark the neighbour when it is queued, not when it is taken out.
narration.28: It is one edge further from k than the current node.
